thread.title: Why Apple Stock Could Be In for a Clobbering

author: Teresa Rivas
title: Why Apple Stock Could Be In for a Clobbering
text:
Illustration: Getty Images By Teresa Rivas Aug. 20, 2018 4:06 p.m. ET Shares of Apple (ticker: AAPL) have outperformed the broader market, the tech sector in general, and fellow FAANG components Facebook (FB) and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) since the start of the year in its journey to become the first company with a $1 trillion market capitalization . But at least one analyst thinks that the good times may not last.
Where we were : Apple has risen 27.3% since the start of the year, nearly double the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF 's (XLK) 14.3% gain, and it's remained popular with smart-money players like hedge funds even when other tech stars have fallen out of favor .
Where we're headed : Potentially lower, argues New Street Research , if iPhone sales disappoint next year.
Amid a tumultuous year for tech, investors have still been hungry for Apple (AAPL). The shares have easily outpaced their tech peers and half of their counterparts in the FAANG group, which also includes Facebook , Amazon.com (AMZN), Netflix (NFLX), and Alphabet. Facebook is in negative territory for 2018 and Google has gained just over 15%. There's been no shortage of naysayers , but despite some big earnings disappointments , tech has still been the best- performing sector this year, helped most recently by Apple's third-quarter earnings .
Apple reached a market value of $1 trillion on Thursday, propelled by the sustained success of the iPhone. WSJ's Spencer Jakab takes a look at how Apple got here. Photo illustration: Heather Seidel/The Wall Street Journal Sales of the iPhone and its selling price were among the elements that investors cheered in Apple's results, but those factors weren't entirely good news, argues New Street Research's Pierre Ferragu . He downgraded Apple to Sell on Monday, with a $165 price target, saying he believes it will be hard to replicate the third quarter's stellar revenues.
Ferragu writes that while the iPhone X has been "successful and well received" by customers, that success is a double-edged sword in that it has brought forward demand at a time when the market is going longer between glitzy new phones that can persuade consumers to trade up. As such, he says, 2019 might be a disappointing year for Apple: "Demand brought forward this year will drive an 'air pocket', and the introduction of a lower-price premium OLED phone won’t be enough to make up for the shortfall."
He argues that Apple is in a transition period, with customers getting new phones less frequently, and that while the company has combated this trend admirably, it has still resulted in boom-and-bust sales cycles. Next year will be a lean year, thanks to the iPhone X's popularity, and while other products in its portfolio will soften the blow a bit, the iPhone has historically been the primary focus for investors. "History shows the stock suffers materially when iPhone revenues disappoint," Ferragu says.
Still, Ferragu is willing to reconsider his stance—after the shares cool off. He says he is "constructive on Apple’s future: the company is in a strong position, will maintain pricing power and grow service revenues, potentially offering good returns, but off a lower stock price."
Apple was down 1% to $215.46 in late trading.
